  "name": "switchboard-starter",
  "private": true,
  "description": "Starter for the Switchboard build round. The harness is given; the product is yours.",
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=22"
  },
  "scripts": {
    "up": "docker compose up -d && node harness/doctor.js --wait",
    "up:search": "docker compose --profile search up -d && node harness/doctor.js --wait",
    "down": "docker compose --profile search down",
    "mocks": "node harness/run-mocks.js",
    "doctor": "node harness/doctor.js",
    "check": "node harness/check.js",
    "check:full": "node harness/check.js --full",
    "chaos": "node harness/pigeon.js chaos",
    "report": "node harness/pigeon.js report",
    "inbound": "node harness/pigeon.js inbound",
    "quiet": "node harness/pigeon.js quiet",
    "drizzle": "node harness/pigeon.js drizzle",
    "scaffold:install": "npm --prefix scaffold/server install && npm --prefix scaffold/web install",
    "scaffold:server": "npm --prefix scaffold/server run dev",
    "scaffold:web": "npm --prefix scaffold/web run dev",
    "start:server": "npm --prefix scaffold/server start"
  }
}

# Switchboard — build round

Build the first version of **Switchboard**, a shared team inbox. Customers
write to a business over a messaging provider. Support agents (people who work
at that business) log in, see conversations arrive in real time, reply, and
leave private notes for each other.

Several businesses (workspaces) use the same deployment. They must never see
each other's data.

**You will not finish everything below.** That is intended. Build the product
first, then make it survive: a small product that keeps working when the
network is bad, the process dies or a second copy is started beats a large one
that works only on the happy path.

Use any AI tools you like. You own every line you submit: in the follow-up
call we open your code, ask why it is the way it is, and debug it with you.

## The two hours

| Time | What |
| --- | --- |
| 0:00 – 0:10 | Read `START_HERE.md` and this brief. Start the services. |
| 0:10 – 1:50 | Build. Commit at least every 15 minutes. |
| 1:50 – 2:00 | Run the full check, push, make the repository public, send the form. See `SUBMISSION.md`. |

The form closes at 2:00. What counts is the commit you name in the form.

## How it fits together

```
simulated customers -> Pigeon :4010 --webhook POST--> YOUR SERVER --WebSocket--> YOUR REACT APP
        (given)          (given)                      (you build)                 (you build)

agent types a reply -> YOUR SERVER -> POST /v1/messages on Pigeon -> status webhooks back to you
```

You build the business side only. The customers are simulated and live inside
Pigeon; there is no customer app, and they do not answer your replies.

| Service | Port | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pigeon | 4010 | The messaging provider (simulated). Sends you webhooks, accepts your sends. Unreliable on purpose. See `PIGEON.md`. |
| Mock IdP | 4020 | OpenID Connect provider with five test users. Discovery at `/.well-known/openid-configuration`. Client id `switchboard-web`. PKCE (S256) is required. |
| MongoDB | 27017 | Real. |
| Redis | 6379 | Real. |
| Elasticsearch | 9200 | Real, optional: `npm run up:search`. |
| Paybox | 4030 | Simulated payment provider. Only for the bonus. See `PAYBOX.md`. |

`scaffold/` is an optional empty shell (Express + TypeScript server, Vite +
React app, already pointed at the services). It has no product code. Use it,
or delete it and bring your own Node stack; then change the `start` command in
`switchboard.json`.

## What to build

### The product
1. **Login.** Sign in through the IdP (authorization code + PKCE). A user's
   workspaces and roles come from the `workspaces` claim. Roles: `admin`, `agent`.
2. **Receive messages.** Accept Pigeon webhooks at `POST /webhooks/pigeon`.
   Pigeon is not a friendly network: read `PIGEON.md` before you write this.
3. **Inbox.** Conversations per contact, newest activity first, paginated.
   Open a conversation and read its messages in order. An agent can claim a
   conversation; two agents cannot both hold it. Close and reopen.
4. **Reply.** An agent replies and the message goes out through Pigeon. The
   agent sees its status: queued, sent, delivered, failed. A customer must
   never receive the same reply twice, and a reply must not be lost.
5. **Real time.** New messages, status changes and assignments appear without
   a refresh (WebSockets). A client that drops and reconnects misses nothing.
6. **Frontend.** A React app an agent could actually use for the above.

### Making it survive: the five levels
The automatic check has five levels. Each is worth points on its own. You can
run all of them yourself except level 4.

| Level | Situation | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | One copy of your server. Webhooks arrive duplicated, out of order, forged and replayed. Pigeon rate-limits you, answers slowly, and goes down for a while. Six agents claim one conversation in the same instant. | 24 |
| 2 | Your server is **killed without warning** (`kill -9`) and started again a few seconds later: once in the middle of a flood of webhooks, once just after it accepted a batch of replies. Nothing may be lost, duplicated or sent twice. | 14 |
| 3 | **Several copies** of your server run behind a load balancer and share MongoDB and Redis. Everything in level 1 must still hold, the rate limit is per workspace and not per copy, and when one copy dies for good the others finish its work within 60 seconds. | 22 |
| 4 | **The written rules.** Not in the check you can run. We send your server the awkward cases that `PIGEON.md` ("How your endpoint must answer") and the contract below describe in words. Ten rules, one point each. | 10 |
| 5 | **Login, tenant isolation and real time**, with several copies running. The check signs in through the IdP as a browser would, calls your API as a user of one workspace, and listens on your WebSocket while customers write. | 15 |

### Also valued (reviewed, not checked automatically)
- **Private notes, end-to-end encrypted.** Agents leave a note on a
  conversation for other agents in the workspace. The server stores it but
  must not be able to read it. Write `PROTOCOL.md`: who holds which key, what
  the server stores, and three attacks your scheme does **not** stop.
- **Tests** for the two or three pieces of logic most likely to be wrong.
- **Search** over messages with Elasticsearch, limited to the user's workspace.
- **Bonus: billing.** Per-seat subscriptions through Paybox. Scored separately
  (10 bonus points). See `BONUS_BILLING.md`. Last, if at all.

## The contract the check relies on

Keep these exactly as written. Everything else about your API is yours.

**A. `switchboard.json`** in the repository root holds the command that starts
your server from a clean clone after `install`. The check runs it itself.

```json
{ "install": "npm run scaffold:install", "start": "npm --prefix scaffold/server start", "health": "/healthz" }
```

**B. Configuration comes from the environment.** Your server listens on the
port in `PORT` and reads every URL and secret from the variables in
`.env.example`. Hard-coded ports or URLs will fail the check. The health path
answers `200` once the server is ready for traffic, and the check waits for that.

**C. Webhook path:** `POST /webhooks/pigeon`.

**D. Check endpoints**, protected by header `x-grader-token` equal to the env
var `GRADER_TOKEN`; without it, or with a wrong one, they answer `401`. They must go through the same code paths your UI uses.

| Endpoint | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /__grader/reset` | Delete all application data, in MongoDB and Redis (login sessions may stay). Answer `200`. |
| `GET /__grader/snapshot` | Return what your system currently believes (shape below). |
| `POST /__grader/reply` `{ workspace, contact, text, client_ref }` | Send a reply to that contact as if an agent typed it, using the given `client_ref` with Pigeon. The contact may not have written yet: the reply still goes out and a conversation now exists. Answer `202` once it is safely stored. The same `client_ref` asked twice, even at the same instant, is one reply and both requests get `202`. A workspace that does not exist is a `4xx`. |
| `POST /__grader/claim` `{ workspace, contact, agent }` | Agent claims that contact's conversation. `200` if this agent now holds it, `409` if someone else does. The holder claiming again gets `200`. If the contact has not written yet, the claim creates the conversation. `agent` is an opaque id; do not look it up in the IdP. |

**E. Login and API**, used by level 5 and by your own frontend.

| Endpoint | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /auth/login` | Redirects the browser to the IdP (authorization code + PKCE). |
| `GET /auth/callback` | Finishes the login and sets a session cookie. |
| `GET /api/me` | `200 { "sub": "u_ben", "workspaces": [{ "id": "ws_acme", "role": "agent" }] }` with a session, `401` without. |
| `GET /api/conversations?workspace=<id>` | The inbox list, in any shape you like. `200` for a member of that workspace, `403` for a signed-in user who is not a member, `401` without a session. |

**F. WebSocket:** `GET /ws?workspace=<id>`, authenticated by the same session
cookie. Refuse the upgrade without a session, or for a workspace the user is
not a member of. Send JSON text frames. Every frame that reports a change
carries `seq`, an integer that only goes up within a workspace:

```json
{ "seq": 41, "type": "message.inbound", "contact": "+14155550101", "message_id": "pmsg_00001ab12" }
{ "seq": 42, "type": "message.status", "contact": "+14155550101", "client_ref": "<ref>", "status": "delivered" }
{ "seq": 43, "type": "conversation.assigned", "contact": "+14155550101", "assignee": "u_ben" }
```

Add any other fields you need. `GET /ws?workspace=<id>&after=41` first sends
every frame after 41 that the client missed, then continues live. With several
copies running, a browser connected to one copy must receive what another
copy processed.

The snapshot shape:

```json
{
  "workspaces": {
    "ws_acme": {
      "contacts": {
        "+14155550101": { "inbound": ["pmsg_00001ab12", "pmsg_00007cd34"], "assignee": "u_ben" }
      },
      "outbound": { "<client_ref>": "delivered" }
    }
  }
}
```

`inbound` is the list of Pigeon `message_id`s for that contact, in the order
your UI shows them, oldest first. `assignee` is who holds the conversation, or
`null`. `outbound` maps the `client_ref` of each message you sent to its
current status.

## Checking yourself

The check is the same program we run on your final commit. We run it with
larger numbers, three copies, different timing, and level 4 added. Reading
`harness/check.js` is allowed and sensible.
Do the levels in the order 1, 5, 2, 3: a product people can log in to comes
before one that survives a crash.

```
npm run check         # level 1 only, about 90 seconds
npm run check:full    # levels 1, 2, 3 and 5, about 4 minutes, writes CHECK_REPORT.json
npm run check -- --levels 5     # one level on its own (or several: --levels 1,5)
```

Stop your own dev server first: the check starts your server itself (from
`switchboard.json`) behind a small load balancer on port 4000. **It deletes
your application data.** Server output goes to `.check-logs/`.

## How you are scored

| | Points |
| --- | --- |
| The check: levels 1 to 5 | 24 + 14 + 22 + 10 + 15 = **85** |
| Security beyond the check: sessions, secrets, encrypted notes if attempted | 4 |
| Data model, structure, code quality and tests | 5 |
| The frontend, and what you chose to build and cut | 3 |
| How you worked with AI (from `ai-logs/`) | 3 |

A submission whose check cannot start scores 0 of 85, so keep
`npm run check` working from your first hour on.

## What the repository must contain

- The code, with history.
- `README.md`: how to run it from a clean clone.
- `switchboard.json`: correct `install` and `start` commands.
- `DECISIONS.md`, half a page: what you built, what you cut and why, what you
  assumed where this brief is silent, and **what you know is still wrong**.
  An honest "level 3 loses replies when a copy dies; I think it is the lock"
  is worth more than silence.
- `CHECK_REPORT.json`: written by your last `npm run check:full`.
- `ai-logs/`: exported transcripts of every AI session you used. Required:
  without them the AI part scores 0 and your submission goes to manual review.
- `PROTOCOL.md`, only if you attempted encrypted notes.

This brief leaves several things unsaid. When you hit one, decide, write the
decision in `DECISIONS.md`, and move on. Questions go in the question channel;
answers go to everyone.

# Pigeon — provider contract

Base URL `http://localhost:4010`. Workspaces and API keys:

| Workspace | API key |
| --- | --- |
| `ws_acme` | `pk_acme_7d1f0a` |
| `ws_globex` | `pk_globex_c93b22` |

Webhook signing secret: `whsec_pigeon_dev`.

## Who is on the other end

Nobody real. Pigeon contains twelve simulated customers, six per workspace,
and a small set of canned texts. It picks one and posts it to you as if that
person had just written to the business. There is no customer app to build.
Customers do not answer your replies; they write on their own schedule.
Nothing you send goes anywhere: Pigeon records it and reports a status.

| Workspace | Simulated customers |
| --- | --- |
| `ws_acme` | +14155550101, +14155550102, +14155550103, +12125550104, +12125550105, +13035550106 |
| `ws_globex` | +442079460201, +442079460202, +442079460203, +4930901820204, +34600111205, +34600111206 |

## Webhooks Pigeon sends you

`POST <your url>` (default `http://localhost:4000/webhooks/pigeon`)

Headers:

- `x-pigeon-signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex>` where `v1` is
  HMAC-SHA256 of `"<t>.<raw request body>"` with the signing secret.
- `x-pigeon-event-id: <event id>`

Body, a contact wrote in:

```json
{ "id": "evt_...", "type": "message.inbound", "workspace": "ws_acme",
  "occurred_at": "2026-11-18T09:30:00.123Z",
  "data": { "message_id": "pmsg_...", "from": "+14155550101", "text": "Hi" } }
```

Body, status of a message you sent:

```json
{ "id": "evt_...", "type": "message.status", "workspace": "ws_acme",
  "occurred_at": "2026-11-18T09:30:02.456Z",
  "data": { "message_id": "pm_...", "client_ref": "<yours>", "status": "sent" } }
```

`status` is `sent`, then `delivered` or `failed`.

What Pigeon promises, and what it does not:

- **At least once.** The same event can arrive several times.
- **No ordering.** Events can arrive in a different order than `occurred_at`.
  `delivered` can arrive before `sent`.
- **Retries.** If you do not answer `2xx` within 5 seconds, Pigeon sends the
  event again: six attempts in all, spread over about 22 seconds. After that
  it is gone. A server that is down for a few seconds therefore loses nothing,
  provided it never answers `2xx` for an event it has not safely stored.
- **Bursts.** Dozens of events in under a second happen.
- **The URL is public.** Anyone can post to it. Pigeon expects you to reject
  requests that are not genuinely from Pigeon, and requests whose timestamp is
  more than five minutes old, with `401`.

### How your endpoint must answer

| Request | Your answer |
| --- | --- |
| Signature missing, malformed, or not matching the raw body | `401`. Never a `5xx`. |
| Signature valid, timestamp more than five minutes old | `401` |
| Signature valid, timestamp up to five minutes old | Genuine. Slow networks exist. |
| Valid event, stored safely (or already stored earlier) | `2xx`, within 5 seconds |
| Valid signature, an event `type` you do not know | `2xx`. Pigeon adds event types without notice, and anything else makes it retry. |
| Valid signature, a status for a message you never sent | `2xx`, and ignore it |
| Valid signature, a body you cannot parse | `400`. Never a `5xx`. |
| Valid signature, a `workspace` you do not know | `2xx`, and ignore it |

## Sending a message

`status` is `sent`, then `delivered` or `failed`.

What Pigeon promises, and what it does not:

- **At least once.** The same event can arrive several times.
- **No ordering.** Events can arrive in a different order than `occurred_at`.
  `delivered` can arrive before `sent`.

  event again: six attempts in all, spread over about 22 seconds. After that
  it is gone. A server that is down for a few seconds therefore loses nothing,
  provided it never answers `2xx` for an event it has not safely stored.
- **Bursts.** Dozens of events in under a second happen.
- **The URL is public.** Anyone can post to it. Pigeon expects you to reject
  requests that are not genuinely from Pigeon, and requests whose timestamp is
  more than five minutes old, with `401`.

| Request | Your answer |
| --- | --- |
| Signature missing, malformed, or not matching the raw body | `401`. Never a `5xx`. |
| Signature valid, timestamp more than five minutes old | `401` |
| Signature valid, timestamp up to five minutes old | Genuine. Slow networks exist. |
| Valid event, stored safely (or already stored earlier) | `2xx`, within 5 seconds |
| Valid signature, an event `type` you do not know | `2xx`. Pigeon adds event types without notice, and anything else makes it retry. |
| Valid signature, a status for a message you never sent | `2xx`, and ignore it |
| Valid signature, a body you cannot parse | `400`. Never a `5xx`. |
| Valid signature, a `workspace` you do not know | `2xx`, and ignore it |

## The big picture
```
   ┌──────────────┐                        ┌──────────────────────┐
   │  CUSTOMER    │  "Hi, my order is late" │   PIGEON  (:4010)    │
   │ (fake, lives │ ──────────────────────▶ │  like WhatsApp/Twilio│
   │ inside Pigeon)│                        │  (given, unreliable) │
   └──────────────┘                        └──────────┬───────────┘
                                                      │ ① sends you the message
                                                      ▼   (webhook)
┌─────────────────┐   ③ live update     ┌──────────────────────────┐
│  AGENT'S BROWSER │ ◀──── WebSocket ─── │     YOUR SERVER          │
│  (React app)     │                     │  (you build this)        │
│                  │ ── ④ "reply" ─────▶ │                          │
└────────┬─────────┘                     └──┬─────────┬──────────┬──┘
         │ login                ② save      │         │ ⑤ send   │
         ▼                                  ▼         │   reply  │
┌─────────────────┐                ┌──────────────┐   ▼          │
│ MOCK IdP (:4020) │                │   MongoDB    │  back to     │
│ "Login with..."  │                │ (all data)   │  PIGEON      │
└─────────────────┘                └──────────────┘              │
                                   ┌──────────────┐              │
                                   │    Redis     │◀─────────────┘
                                   │ (sharing     │  server copies
                                   │ between      │  talk to each
                                   │ copies)      │  other here
                                   └──────────────┘
```

## The story in 5 steps
1. **A customer writes.** Pigeon sends the message to your server at `POST /webhooks/pigeon`.
2. **Your server saves it** in MongoDB, and only then tells Pigeon "OK (200)".
3. **The agent sees it immediately.** Your server pushes it to the browser over a WebSocket, with no page refresh.
4. **The agent types a reply** in the React app.
5. **Your server sends the reply through Pigeon.** Pigeon later reports back: sent ✔, delivered ✔✔, or failed ✖.

**Login** happens before all of this: the agent clicks "Login", picks a user on the IdP page, and comes back logged in.

## Why it's hard: Pigeon is badly behaved on purpose
```
What Pigeon does                       What your server must do
──────────────────────────────────     ─────────────────────────────────────
Sends the same message 3 times    ──▶  Save it once (ignore duplicates)
Sends "delivered" before "sent"   ──▶  Never go backwards: delivered wins
Fake/hacker requests              ──▶  Check signature → reject with 401
Says "too many, slow down" (429)  ──▶  Wait and retry later
Is down for 15 seconds (503)      ──▶  Keep the reply queued, send when back
Takes 12 s to answer (but sent!)  ──▶  Retry with the same key → no double send
```

## Why it's hard: the server gets attacked too
```
Level 2: server killed suddenly        Level 3: many copies of your server

  Server ──X (kill -9)                    Browser ─▶ ┌─────────┐
  ... restarted 5 s later                            │ copy 1  │──┐
                                                     ├─────────┤  │  shared
  Nothing may be lost:                    Pigeon ──▶ │ copy 2  │──┼─▶ Mongo
  → save to Mongo BEFORE saying OK                   ├─────────┤  │    Redis
  → queued replies resume after restart              │ copy 3  │──┘
                                                     └─────────┘
                                          → nothing kept in server memory
                                          → copies share news via Redis
```

## Short version
> Build a **WhatsApp-style team inbox**. Messages come in from Pigeon, agents see them live, claim a conversation and reply. Make sure **nothing is lost or sent twice**, even when Pigeon misbehaves, the server crashes, or 3 copies run at once.

- 4.2 Background sender: atomically take a queued reply and hold it for a limited time, so if a copy dies another copy picks it up within 60 s
- 4.3 Call Pigeon with `Idempotency-Key = client_ref` and a timeout
- 4.4 On 429, 503, timeout or outage: keep it queued and retry later (respect `Retry-After`)
- 4.5 **Rate limit per workspace in Redis** (8 sends, refilling at 4/s), shared by all copies

### Task 5 — Real-time events → Levels 5, 3
- 5.1 Every change creates an event with a `seq` that only goes up within the workspace (a Redis counter), saved in Mongo
- 5.2 Broadcast the event through Redis pub/sub so every server copy receives it
- 5.3 `/ws?workspace=&after=`: check the session and membership, replay missed events, then send live ones

### Task 6 — Login and API → Level 5
- 6.1 `/auth/login`: redirect to the IdP with PKCE (keep `state` and the verifier in Redis)
- 6.2 `/auth/callback`: exchange the code for tokens, read the `workspaces` claim, store the session in Redis, set the cookie
- 6.3 `/api/me` and `/api/conversations?workspace=` with the right 401/403

- 7.2 Inbox list (newest first, paginated)
- 7.3 Conversation view: messages in order, reply box, status ticks (queued, sent, delivered, failed)
- 7.4 Claim, close and reopen buttons
- 7.5 Live updates over the WebSocket, reconnecting with `after=lastSeq`

### Task 8 — Test against the check (keep doing this throughout)
- Run `npm run check` after Tasks 2, 3 and 4
- Run `npm run check -- --levels 5` after Task 6
- `npm run check:full` covers levels 2 and 3

### Task 9 — Submission (at 1:50)

- `README.md`, `DECISIONS.md` (including what you cut and what's still wrong)
- Export the AI chats into `ai-logs/`, push, make the repo public, send the form

- Encrypted notes, Elasticsearch search, Paybox billing. Maybe 1–2 small tests for the status ordering and the signature check.

Task 0 and Task 1 are both finished, committed and pushed (`59c430a`).

## Task 0.5: what the check showed
The check starts our server fine and stopped at `/__grader/reset` returning 404, as expected. Reading [check.js](harness/check.js) taught us these rules for the next tasks:
- **Order inbound messages by Pigeon's `occurred_at`**, not by when they arrive. I changed the database index to match.
- **Never store forged or replayed messages.** Their ids start with `forged_` or `stale_`, and any one stored costs points.
- **Acknowledge webhooks fast:** the 95th-percentile response time must be under 1 second.
- **The claim race:** 6 agents claim each of 5 conversations at the same instant, and exactly one may win each.

## Task 1: what I built ([grader.ts](scaffold/server/src/grader.ts))
| Endpoint | What it does | Tested |
|---|---|---|
| Token check | Every `/__grader/*` request needs the right `x-grader-token`, otherwise **401**. Compared in constant time. | No token → 401, wrong token → 401 ✅ |
| `POST /__grader/reset` | Empties our Mongo collections and deletes our Redis keys (`sb:*`), keeping login sessions | Snapshot is empty afterwards ✅ |
| `GET /__grader/snapshot` | Returns workspaces → contacts → inbound ids (**sorted by occurred_at**) + assignee, plus outbound `client_ref` → status | I inserted p2 before p1 and it still returned `["p1","p2"]` ✅ |

**Next is Task 2, the webhook**, which carries the most points in level 1. Shall I start?

Every webhook test now passes. The remaining 7 points come from Tasks 3 and 4.

## What I built
- **[webhook.ts](scaffold/server/src/webhook.ts)**: checks the signature and the 5-minute timestamp, returning 401 before anything else. Bad JSON gets 400. Unknown event types and workspaces get 200 and are ignored. Each customer message is stored exactly once thanks to the unique index, and if two copies of the same webhook arrive at the same instant, the loser simply retries as an update. A reply's status only moves forward (`delivered` can't go back to `sent`).
- **[events.ts](scaffold/server/src/events.ts)**: `emitEvent()`. It takes the next `seq` from a Mongo counter (one shared counter, so it works across server copies), saves the event, and publishes it to Redis. The WebSocket in Task 5 will plug into it.
- Small changes to [app.ts](scaffold/server/src/app.ts) (the webhook route goes before the JSON parser, because the signature needs the raw body) and [db.ts](scaffold/server/src/db.ts) (the `counters` collection).

1. **Windows problem with the check.** It can't stop the servers it starts, so a copy is left running on port 4001 and the next run fails with a misleading 404. I cleaned it up this time. After each check run, use this in PowerShell:

   ```

2. **`package.json` was changed by something other than me.** A dependency `"switchboard-starter": "file:../.."` was added to both `scaffold/server` and `scaffold/web`, probably by an `npm install` run with unusual arguments. It links the repo to itself and isn't needed. I'd undo it before committing:

   ```
3. **Ready for you to commit:** `TASKS.md`, `app.ts`, `db.ts`, plus the new files `events.ts` and `webhook.ts`. Suggested message:
   `Task 2: signed Pigeon webhook, exactly-once inbound, forward-only status, emitEvent`

A light structure is worth it, but not full MVC. Code quality and structure is only 5 points, and the clock matters more. Still, we're about to add claim, replies, the sender worker, auth and the WebSocket, so a flat `src/` would end up with around 15 files mixed together. In the follow-up call you'll also need to find and explain code quickly.

What I'd skip: separate `models/` and `controllers/` layers. Mongo doesn't need model classes (we use plain documents and indexes), and controller layers add files without adding value in a 2-hour build.

## Proposed structure
```
src/
├── index.ts              start server, workers, graceful shutdown
├── app.ts                Express app: mounts routes, error handler
├── config.ts
├── lib/                  infrastructure, no business rules
│   ├── db.ts             Mongo connect, collections, indexes
│   ├── redis.ts
│   └── http.ts           HttpError, ah(), errorHandler
├── routes/               HTTP only: parse input → call service → send status
│   ├── webhook.ts        POST /webhooks/pigeon (signature + parsing)
│   ├── grader.ts         /__grader/*
│   ├── api.ts            /api/*          (task 6)
│   └── auth.ts           /auth/*         (task 6)
├── services/             business logic, shared by grader routes AND the UI
│   ├── inbound.ts        storeInbound, applyStatus
│   ├── conversations.ts  claim, close/reopen, list      (task 3)
│   ├── replies.ts        queue a reply                  (task 4)
│   └── events.ts         emitEvent
├── workers/
│   └── sender.ts         sends queued replies to Pigeon (task 4)
└── ws.ts                 WebSocket server               (task 5)
```

**The key rule:** routes contain no business logic, and services contain no HTTP code. That matters here because the brief says the grader endpoints must *"go through the same code paths your UI uses"*. So `/__grader/claim` and the UI's claim button both call `services/conversations.claim()`.

Moving the existing files takes about 3 minutes: a few moves, splitting `webhook.ts` into a route and a service, and fixing imports. It's best done now, before Task 3 adds more code. Shall I restructure and then go straight into Task 3? I won't commit.

Task 4 edge cases first:
- **Same `client_ref` twice, even at the same instant** → one reply (unique index) and both requests get 202
- **Server killed right after accepting** → the reply is already stored as `queued` in Mongo, so the worker picks it up after the restart
- **Killed in the middle of a send** → the reply's "lease" expires and another worker (or this one after restart) resends it with the **same `Idempotency-Key`**, so Pigeon never sends twice
- **429** → record a cool-off in Redis that *every* server copy respects, so nothing is sent inside a `Retry-After` window
- **503, timeout, outage** → back to the queue with backoff; never give up
- **Rate limit** → a Redis token bucket per workspace, shared by all copies

## Task 5: high-level diagram
```
   Pigeon webhook / agent reply / claim  (handled by ANY server copy)
                     │
                     ▼
        ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ emitEvent(ws, type, data)          │   (already built in Task 2)
        │  1. seq = counter +1   (Mongo)     │
        │  2. save event         (Mongo)     │──────────┐
        │  3. PUBLISH sb:events:{ws} (Redis) │          │
        └──────────────┬─────────────────────┘          │
                       │ Redis pub/sub                   │ events collection
          ┌────────────┼─────────────┐                   │ {workspace, seq, type, ...}
          ▼            ▼             ▼                   │
   ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐             │
   │ copy 1    │ │ copy 2    │ │ copy 3    │  each copy SUBSCRIBES once
   │ WS hub    │ │ WS hub    │ │ WS hub    │  and forwards to its own sockets
   └─────┬─────┘ └─────┬─────┘ └───────────┘             │
         │ only sockets of that workspace                │
         ▼             ▼                                 │
     Browser A     Browser B ◀── on reconnect: replay ───┘
    (ws_acme)     (ws_acme)       seq > after from Mongo
```

## What happens when a browser connects
```
GET /ws?workspace=ws_acme&after=41    (cookie: sb_session=...)
   │
   ├─ 1. Session from cookie? ─────────── no  → refuse (401, no upgrade)
   ├─ 2. Member of ws_acme? ───────────── no  → refuse (403, no upgrade)
   ├─ 3. Upgrade to WebSocket, start listening to live events (buffer them)
   ├─ 4. Replay from Mongo: events with seq > 41, in order → send
   ├─ 5. Flush buffered live events, skipping seq already sent
   └─ 6. Live: send each new event, only if seq > last sent
```

## Two tricky cases
**1. Events can arrive slightly out of order across copies.** Copy A takes seq 42 and copy B takes seq 43, but B publishes first. The socket would see 43 before 42, and the check fails if seq ever goes down.
→ **Fix:** each socket remembers `lastSent`. If 43 arrives while `lastSent` = 41, there's a gap, so it reads 42–43 from Mongo and sends them in order.

**2. An event published during the replay.** It could be sent twice, or be missed.
→ **Fix:** start listening *before* the replay, buffer what arrives, and skip anything with seq ≤ `lastSent`.

Here's the design, based on how the mock IdP is implemented in `idp/server.js`.

## Task 6: high-level diagram
```
 BROWSER (or the check)        YOUR SERVER (any copy)                 MOCK IdP :4020
 ──────────────────────        ──────────────────────                 ──────────────
 1. GET /auth/login ─────────▶ make state, nonce, code_verifier
                               save {verifier, nonce} in Redis
                                 sb:pkce:{state}  (10 min, single use)
                               set cookie sb_login=state
    ◀──── 302 to IdP ───────── /authorize?client_id&redirect_uri
                                 &code_challenge=SHA256(verifier)
                                 &state&nonce&scope=openid
 2. ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ user picks "Ben"
    ◀──────────────────────── 302 /auth/callback?code=..&state=.. ──── (code valid 60 s)
 3. GET /auth/callback ──────▶ state matches cookie? take it from Redis
                               (GETDEL: a code/state can't be replayed)
                               POST /token {code, code_verifier, ──────▶ checks PKCE
                                            client_secret}        ◀───── id_token (RS256 JWT)
                               verify id_token: signature (JWKS),
                                 iss, aud, exp, nonce
                               session = {sub, name, email, workspaces}
                               save in Redis sb:sess:{random id} (8 h)
    ◀──── 302 to web app ───── Set-Cookie: sb_session=<id>; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
 4. GET /api/me ─────────────▶ cookie → Redis → session    → 200 {sub, workspaces}
                               no/unknown cookie            → 401
 5. GET /api/conversations   ▶ requireSession  → 401
      ?workspace=ws_globex     requireMember(ws) → 403 (Ben isn't in ws_globex)
                               → services/conversations.list()  → 200
 6. WS /ws?workspace=ws_acme ▶ same cookie, same check (already built in Task 5)
```

## Request pipeline for `/api/*`
```
request ─▶ requireSession ─▶ requireMember(workspace) ─▶ route ─▶ SERVICE (same as grader)
             401 if none        403 if not a member        input      claim / reply / list
```

## API endpoints
| Endpoint | Purpose | Calls service |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /auth/login`, `/auth/callback`, `POST /auth/logout` | Sign in and out | `sessions` |
| `GET /api/me` | Who am I, plus my workspaces and roles | – |
| `GET /api/conversations?workspace=&state=&cursor=` | Inbox: newest activity first, **paginated** | `conversations.list` |
| `GET /api/conversations/:contact/messages?workspace=` | Messages in order (in + out with status) | `conversations.messages` |
| `POST /api/conversations/:contact/reply` `{workspace, text, client_ref}` | Reply → 202 | `replies.queueReply` (same as grader) |
| `POST .../claim`, `.../release` | Claim → 200 / 409 | `conversations.claim` (same as grader) |
| `POST .../close`, `.../reopen` | Change state | `conversations.setState` |

The agent id for claims comes from the **session's `sub`**, never from the request body, so nobody can claim on behalf of someone else.

## Security choices (part of the 4 "security" points)
- **PKCE S256 + `state` + `nonce`**: protects the login against stolen codes, CSRF and replayed tokens
- **The id_token is verified** with the IdP's public key (JWKS), not just decoded

- **Workspaces come from the signed token**, never from the client
- Logout deletes the session in Redis

# Decisions (half-page note)

<!-- Add one line the moment you decide something. Tidy it at 1:40. Keep it to about half a page. -->

## How to run
See README.md.

## What I built first and why
- [e.g. Payment flow first: it carries the most risk (double charges) and the checker tests it hardest.]

## Decisions where the brief was silent
- A new customer message on a closed conversation reopens it (keeps the assignee) — the customer needs an answer again.
- Claiming a conversation that does not exist yet creates it (brief requires this for `/__grader/claim`); same rule in the UI.
- Inbox order inside a conversation is Pigeon's `occurred_at`, not arrival time, because webhooks arrive out of order.
- A workspace "exists" if we have a Pigeon API key for it (`PIGEON_KEY_WS_*`); unknown workspaces in webhooks are acknowledged and ignored.

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| [App.tsx](scaffold/web/src/App.tsx) | Sign-in screen, workspace picker, open/closed/all tabs, inbox with "Load more", and the conversation view with status ticks (🕓 queued, ✓ sent, ✓✓ delivered, ✗ failed). It has Claim, Release, Close and Reopen buttons, and shows a 409 as "Someone else already holds this conversation". |
| [useLive.ts](scaffold/web/src/useLive.ts) | The WebSocket. It **reconnects with backoff using `after=lastSeq`** so nothing is missed, ignores duplicate frames, and shows a "● Live / Reconnecting…" indicator. |
| [api.ts](scaffold/web/src/api.ts) | A typed API client with a 10 s timeout |
| Replies | Each message gets **one `client_ref`** when you press Send. It's retried up to 3 times with the same ref, so you never get a double reply. If it can't be saved, it shows "not saved · retry" and the text is kept. |
| Server | A new `GET /api/conversations/:contact` endpoint, so the conversation view shows the correct assignee and state |

# Decisions

## What I built, in this order, and why
1. **Webhook intake** (signature, dedupe, ordering) and the grader endpoints first: everything else depends on messages being stored exactly once, and the check needs `reset`/`snapshot` to see anything.
2. **Claim** (one atomic Mongo update) and **replies** (stored as `queued`, then sent by a leased background worker): this is where loss and double-sends happen.
3. **Realtime** (event log + Redis fan-out) and **OIDC login**, then the **React inbox**.

Result: full check (levels 1, 2, 3, 5) **75/75** — see "Check report on Windows" below for how that was measured.

## How it handles failure
- **Duplicates / replays**: unique indexes — inbound on `(workspace, message_id)`, outbound on `(workspace, client_ref)`, conversation on `(workspace, contact)`. Concurrent upserts that lose with E11000 are retried as updates.
- **Forged / stale webhooks**: HMAC over the raw body, constant-time compare, timestamp within 5 min → else `401`. Unparseable → `400`. Unknown type/workspace/client_ref → `2xx` and ignored. `2xx` only after the write.
- **Out-of-order statuses**: status has a rank (`queued < sent < delivered = failed`); updates only move forward.
- **Pigeon slow / 503 / outage**: 4 s timeout, retry forever with capped backoff; every attempt uses `Idempotency-Key = client_ref`, so a send that "timed out" but succeeded is not sent again.
- **Rate limit**: a token bucket per workspace in Redis (Lua, Redis clock), shared by all copies, set below Pigeon's limit. A `429` sets a per-workspace cool-off in Redis that every copy respects.
- **Process killed**: a reply is in Mongo before `202`. The worker leases a job for 15 s; if the copy dies, the lease expires and any copy resends it (same idempotency key).
- **Several copies**: no state in memory. `seq` comes from an atomic Mongo counter; events are stored in Mongo and fanned out with Redis pub/sub; each socket fills gaps from Mongo so `seq` never goes backwards. Sessions and PKCE state are in Redis.

## Decisions where the brief was silent
- A new customer message on a closed conversation reopens it (assignee kept).
- `admin` and `agent` have the same rights; the brief defines no difference.
- In the UI an agent claims as themselves (`sub` from the session); the body never names the agent.
- A workspace exists if there is a Pigeon API key for it (`PIGEON_KEY_WS_*`).
- Message order is Pigeon's `occurred_at`; outbound messages use the time we accepted them.
- Sessions: random 256-bit id, HttpOnly + SameSite=Lax cookie, data in Redis for 8 h. id_token verified (RS256/JWKS, iss, aud, exp, nonce); PKCE S256; `state` single-use and bound to the browser by a cookie.

## What I cut, and what that means
- **Encrypted notes, Elasticsearch search, Paybox billing**: not built. No notes feature at all; no search; no billing.
- **Automated tests**: none written; I relied on the provided check plus scripted manual tests. The first ones I would add: status ordering, webhook signature/timestamp, claim race.
- **Message pagination** inside a conversation (capped at the latest 500) and a last-message preview in the inbox list.

## Known problems
- **Realtime gap fill**: if another copy's event takes more than ~0.5 s to be written, a live socket skips it (it is still in Mongo; the UI reloads on reconnect, but that socket never receives that frame).
- **Crash between storing an inbound message and emitting its event**: on Pigeon's retry the event is emitted then — but if the crash came after emitting and before marking it, the event is emitted twice (two seqs, same `message_id`). The UI reloads, so it only shows once.
- **A status webhook Pigeon gives up on** (6 attempts) leaves the reply at `queued`/`sent` forever: there is no reconciliation with Pigeon.
- The `events` collection grows without limit (no TTL / compaction).
- A user's workspaces are read at login; role changes in the IdP apply only after the next login (≤ 8 h).

## Check report on Windows
`harness/check.js` kills servers with `process.kill(-pid)`, which does nothing on Windows: the "killed" server keeps port 4001, the restart fails with `EADDRINUSE`, and the check stops at level 2 with `502`. So the unmodified run (`CHECK_REPORT.json`) shows **24/75** (level 1 complete, then stopped).
To test levels 2 and 3 for real I ran a local copy whose only change is that kill (`taskkill` on the process tree and on whatever listens on the instance port): `scripts/make-check-win.js` makes that copy. Its full run is `CHECK_REPORT.windows-patched.json`: **75/75**. On Linux the unmodified check should behave like the patched one.

## Pre-prepared material
Before the session I wrote generic templates (`CLAUDE.md`, `PLAN.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, a task-list format), committed separately right after the starter. No product code was prepared in advance.

## AI usage
Claude Code (transcripts in `ai-logs/`). I asked for a design and edge cases before each task, had the structure changed to `lib/ routes/ services/ workers/`, reviewed each step, and ran the check after every task.

stop and restart them.

# Design: data model and API

Architecture diagram and build order: `TASKS.md`. Choices and known problems: `DECISIONS.md`.

## MongoDB

### `conversations` — one per contact per workspace
| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| workspace, contact | **unique** `(workspace, contact)` |
| assignee | agent id or `null`; set only by the atomic claim |
| state | `open` / `closed` |
| lastActivityAt | `$max` of message times; inbox index `(workspace, lastActivityAt desc)` |

### `messages` — inbound and outbound in one collection
| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| direction | `in` / `out` |
| workspace, contact, text, occurredAt | order index `(workspace, contact, occurredAt)` |
| providerMessageId | inbound: **unique** `(workspace, providerMessageId)` where `direction=in` |
| evented | inbound: realtime event already emitted |
| clientRef | outbound: **unique** `(workspace, clientRef)` where `direction=out` |
| status, statusRank | outbound, visible: `queued → sent → delivered / failed`; only moves forward |
| sendState, nextAttemptAt, leaseOwner, attempts | outbound, worker: `pending → sending (lease) → accepted / rejected`; index `(sendState, nextAttemptAt)` |
| author | outbound: agent `sub`, or `null` for the grader |

### `events` — realtime log for replay
`{ workspace, seq, type, contact, ... }`, **unique** `(workspace, seq)`.

### `counters`
`{ _id: "seq:<workspace>", seq }` — atomic `$inc` gives the next `seq`.

## Redis (all keys `sb:*`)
| Key | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `sb:sess:<id>` | session `{sub, name, email, workspaces}`, 8 h (kept by `/__grader/reset`) |
| `sb:pkce:<state>` | login in progress `{verifier, nonce}`, 10 min, single use |
| `sb:rl:<ws>` | token bucket for sends to Pigeon |
| `sb:cooloff:<ws>` | no sends until this time (after a `429`) |
| channel `sb:events:<ws>` | pub/sub fan-out of events to every copy |

## HTTP
| Method | Path | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/healthz` | 200 when ready, 503 while shutting down |
| POST | `/webhooks/pigeon` | signed; 401 / 400 / 2xx rules from `PIGEON.md` |
| POST | `/__grader/reset`, `/reply`, `/claim`; GET `/snapshot` | `x-grader-token` |
| GET | `/auth/login`, `/auth/callback`; POST `/auth/logout` | OIDC code + PKCE |
| GET | `/api/me` | 401 without session |
| GET | `/api/conversations?workspace=&state=&cursor=&limit=` | inbox, newest first; 403 if not a member |
| GET | `/api/conversations/:contact?workspace=` | one conversation |
| GET | `/api/conversations/:contact/messages?workspace=` | oldest first |
| POST | `/api/conversations/:contact/reply?workspace=` `{text, client_ref}` | 202; same `client_ref` = same reply |
| POST | `/api/conversations/:contact/claim` · `release` · `close` · `reopen` `?workspace=` | claim 200 / 409 |
| WS | `/ws?workspace=&after=` | session cookie; frames `{seq, type, ...}` |

# Decisions

## What I built, in this order, and why
1. **Webhook intake** (signature, dedupe, ordering) and the grader endpoints first: everything else depends on messages being stored exactly once, and the check needs `reset`/`snapshot` to see anything.
2. **Claim** (one atomic Mongo update) and **replies** (stored as `queued`, then sent by a leased background worker): this is where loss and double-sends happen.
3. **Realtime** (event log + Redis fan-out) and **OIDC login**, then the **React inbox**.

Result: full check (levels 1, 2, 3, 5) **75/75** — see "Check report on Windows" below for how that was measured.

## How it handles failure
- **Duplicates / replays**: unique indexes — inbound on `(workspace, message_id)`, outbound on `(workspace, client_ref)`, conversation on `(workspace, contact)`. Concurrent upserts that lose with E11000 are retried as updates.
- **Forged / stale webhooks**: HMAC over the raw body, constant-time compare, timestamp within 5 min → else `401`. Unparseable → `400`. Unknown type/workspace/client_ref → `2xx` and ignored. `2xx` only after the write.
- **Out-of-order statuses**: status has a rank (`queued < sent < delivered = failed`); updates only move forward.
- **Pigeon slow / 503 / outage**: 4 s timeout, retry forever with capped backoff; every attempt uses `Idempotency-Key = client_ref`, so a send that "timed out" but succeeded is not sent again.
- **Rate limit**: a token bucket per workspace in Redis (Lua, Redis clock), shared by all copies, set below Pigeon's limit. A `429` sets a per-workspace cool-off in Redis that every copy respects.
- **Process killed**: a reply is in Mongo before `202`. The worker leases a job for 15 s; if the copy dies, the lease expires and any copy resends it (same idempotency key).
- **Several copies**: no state in memory. `seq` comes from an atomic Mongo counter; events are stored in Mongo and fanned out with Redis pub/sub; each socket fills gaps from Mongo so `seq` never goes backwards. Sessions and PKCE state are in Redis.

## Decisions where the brief was silent
- A new customer message on a closed conversation reopens it (assignee kept).
- `admin` and `agent` have the same rights; the brief defines no difference.
- In the UI an agent claims as themselves (`sub` from the session); the body never names the agent.
- A workspace exists if there is a Pigeon API key for it (`PIGEON_KEY_WS_*`).
- Message order is Pigeon's `occurred_at`; outbound messages use the time we accepted them.
- Sessions: random 256-bit id, HttpOnly + SameSite=Lax cookie, data in Redis for 8 h. id_token verified (RS256/JWKS, iss, aud, exp, nonce); PKCE S256; `state` single-use and bound to the browser by a cookie.

## What I cut, and what that means
- **Encrypted notes, Elasticsearch search, Paybox billing**: not built. No notes feature at all; no search; no billing.
- **Automated tests**: none written; I relied on the provided check plus scripted manual tests. The first ones I would add: status ordering, webhook signature/timestamp, claim race.
- **Message pagination** inside a conversation (capped at the latest 500) and a last-message preview in the inbox list.

## Known problems
- **Realtime gap fill**: if another copy's event takes more than ~0.5 s to be written, a live socket skips it (it is still in Mongo; the UI reloads on reconnect, but that socket never receives that frame).
- **Crash between storing an inbound message and emitting its event**: on Pigeon's retry the event is emitted then — but if the crash came after emitting and before marking it, the event is emitted twice (two seqs, same `message_id`). The UI reloads, so it only shows once.
- **A status webhook Pigeon gives up on** (6 attempts) leaves the reply at `queued`/`sent` forever: there is no reconciliation with Pigeon.
- The `events` collection grows without limit (no TTL / compaction).
- A user's workspaces are read at login; role changes in the IdP apply only after the next login (≤ 8 h).

## Check report on Windows
`harness/check.js` kills servers with `process.kill(-pid)`, which does nothing on Windows: the "killed" server keeps port 4001, the restart fails with `EADDRINUSE`, and the check stops at level 2 with `502`. So the unmodified run (`CHECK_REPORT.json`) shows **24/75** (level 1 complete, then stopped).
To test levels 2 and 3 for real I ran a local copy whose only change is that kill (`taskkill` on the process tree and on whatever listens on the instance port): `scripts/make-check-win.js` makes that copy. Its full run is `CHECK_REPORT.windows-patched.json`: **75/75**. On Linux the unmodified check should behave like the patched one.

## Pre-prepared material
Before the session I wrote generic templates (`CLAUDE.md`, `PLAN.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, a task-list format), committed separately right after the starter. No product code was prepared in advance.

## AI usage
Claude Code (transcripts in `ai-logs/`). I asked for a design and edge cases before each task, had the structure changed to `lib/ routes/ services/ workers/`, reviewed each step, and ran the check after every task.

## How to run
See README.md.

## What I built first and why
- [e.g. Payment flow first: it carries the most risk (double charges) and the checker tests it hardest.]

## Decisions where the brief was silent
- A new customer message on a closed conversation reopens it (keeps the assignee) — the customer needs an answer again.
- Claiming a conversation that does not exist yet creates it (brief requires this for `/__grader/claim`); same rule in the UI.
- Inbox order inside a conversation is Pigeon's `occurred_at`, not arrival time, because webhooks arrive out of order.
- A workspace "exists" if we have a Pigeon API key for it (`PIGEON_KEY_WS_*`); unknown workspaces in webhooks are acknowledged and ignored.
- Roles: `admin` and `agent` can do the same things for now (claim, reply, close); the brief does not define a difference.
- In the UI an agent claims as themselves (`sub` from the session); the body can never name another agent.
- Sessions: random 256-bit id in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookie; data in Redis (8 h) so every copy sees it. id_token verified (RS256 via JWKS, iss, aud, exp, nonce); login uses PKCE S256 + state bound to the browser by a cookie.
- Realtime `seq` comes from an atomic Mongo counter (not Redis) so it survives a Redis restart and stays unique across server copies.

# Switchboard

A shared team inbox. Customers write through Pigeon (a simulated messaging provider); support agents sign in,
see conversations arrive in real time, claim them, reply, and close them. Several workspaces share one deployment
and never see each other's data. Built to keep working when the network is bad, a process is killed, or several
copies run at once.

## Run from a clean clone

Requires **Node 22** and **Docker** (or your own MongoDB and Redis).

```bash
npm run up                  # MongoDB, Redis, Pigeon, mock IdP, Paybox (Docker) and a health check
npm run scaffold:install    # install server + web dependencies (same as switchboard.json "install")

npm run scaffold:server     # API + webhook + WebSocket on http://localhost:4000
npm run scaffold:web        # React app on http://localhost:5173  (open this)
```

Sign in on the mock IdP page by clicking a user (no passwords). Eli Novak belongs to both workspaces.
Customer messages arrive every few seconds; `npm run inbound` sends one now, `npm run quiet` / `npm run drizzle`
stop and restart them.

No Docker: `npm run mocks` starts the simulators with plain Node; set `MONGO_URL` and `REDIS_URL`.

Configuration comes only from the environment (defaults in `.env.example`, optional `.env` in the repo root).
The server listens on `PORT`.

## Check

Stop your dev server first: the check starts the server itself and **deletes application data**.

```bash
npm run check          # level 1
npm run check:full     # levels 1, 2, 3, 5 -> CHECK_REPORT.json
```

On Windows the check cannot kill the server (see `DECISIONS.md`); `scripts/make-check-win.js` makes a local
copy with that one line fixed. Results: `CHECK_REPORT.json` (unmodified, Windows) and
`CHECK_REPORT.windows-patched.json` (75/75).

## How it works

```
Pigeon --signed webhook--> /webhooks/pigeon --> Mongo (unique ids) --> emitEvent: seq + event log + Redis pub/sub
Agent  --reply---------->  /api/.../reply   --> Mongo "queued" (202) --> sender worker (any copy, leased)
                                                 --> rate limit (Redis) --> Pigeon /v1/messages (Idempotency-Key)
Browser <--WebSocket /ws?workspace=&after=  <-- replay from Mongo, then live from Redis (any copy)
```

Server code (`scaffold/server/src`):

| Folder | What |
| --- | --- |
| `routes/` | HTTP only: `webhook.ts`, `grader.ts`, `auth.ts` (OIDC), `api.ts` (UI API, 401/403) |
| `services/` | Business logic shared by the UI and grader routes: inbound, conversations (claim), replies, events, sessions |
| `workers/sender.ts` | Sends queued replies; retries, `Retry-After`, failover via leases |
| `lib/` | Mongo (indexes), Redis, Pigeon client, rate limiter, OIDC, errors |
| `ws.ts` | WebSocket hub: auth on upgrade, replay, live fan-out, gap fill |

Web app (`scaffold/web/src`): `App.tsx` (inbox, conversation, reply, claim/close), `useLive.ts` (WebSocket with
reconnect + `after=`), `api.ts`.

More: `DECISIONS.md` (choices, cuts, known problems), `PLAN.md` (data model and API), `TASKS.md` (build order).

# Design: data model and API

Architecture diagram and build order: `TASKS.md`. Choices and known problems: `DECISIONS.md`.

## MongoDB

### `conversations` — one per contact per workspace
| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| workspace, contact | **unique** `(workspace, contact)` |
| assignee | agent id or `null`; set only by the atomic claim |
| state | `open` / `closed` |
| lastActivityAt | `$max` of message times; inbox index `(workspace, lastActivityAt desc)` |

### `messages` — inbound and outbound in one collection
| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| direction | `in` / `out` |
| workspace, contact, text, occurredAt | order index `(workspace, contact, occurredAt)` |
| providerMessageId | inbound: **unique** `(workspace, providerMessageId)` where `direction=in` |
| evented | inbound: realtime event already emitted |
| clientRef | outbound: **unique** `(workspace, clientRef)` where `direction=out` |
| status, statusRank | outbound, visible: `queued → sent → delivered / failed`; only moves forward |
| sendState, nextAttemptAt, leaseOwner, attempts | outbound, worker: `pending → sending (lease) → accepted / rejected`; index `(sendState, nextAttemptAt)` |
| author | outbound: agent `sub`, or `null` for the grader |

### `events` — realtime log for replay
`{ workspace, seq, type, contact, ... }`, **unique** `(workspace, seq)`.

### `counters`
`{ _id: "seq:<workspace>", seq }` — atomic `$inc` gives the next `seq`.

## Redis (all keys `sb:*`)
| Key | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `sb:sess:<id>` | session `{sub, name, email, workspaces}`, 8 h (kept by `/__grader/reset`) |
| `sb:pkce:<state>` | login in progress `{verifier, nonce}`, 10 min, single use |
| `sb:rl:<ws>` | token bucket for sends to Pigeon |
| `sb:cooloff:<ws>` | no sends until this time (after a `429`) |
| channel `sb:events:<ws>` | pub/sub fan-out of events to every copy |

## HTTP
| Method | Path | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/healthz` | 200 when ready, 503 while shutting down |
| POST | `/webhooks/pigeon` | signed; 401 / 400 / 2xx rules from `PIGEON.md` |
| POST | `/__grader/reset`, `/reply`, `/claim`; GET `/snapshot` | `x-grader-token` |
| GET | `/auth/login`, `/auth/callback`; POST `/auth/logout` | OIDC code + PKCE |
| GET | `/api/me` | 401 without session |
| GET | `/api/conversations?workspace=&state=&cursor=&limit=` | inbox, newest first; 403 if not a member |
| GET | `/api/conversations/:contact?workspace=` | one conversation |
| GET | `/api/conversations/:contact/messages?workspace=` | oldest first |
| POST | `/api/conversations/:contact/reply?workspace=` `{text, client_ref}` | 202; same `client_ref` = same reply |
| POST | `/api/conversations/:contact/claim` · `release` · `close` · `reopen` `?workspace=` | claim 200 / 409 |
| WS | `/ws?workspace=&after=` | session cookie; frames `{seq, type, ...}` |
